risk_of_bias.note: The comparison that carries the claim, MDMA against placebo in the same people, is at worst some concerns on the cards (session order is not described in the Basel pooled paper, the three-site paper or the Chicago paper), but the ratings are self-reports by volunteers who could tell what they had been given: the effects are obvious, the Basel authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had, and no paper tested the blind. The Basel papers also tested about 40 to 60 outcomes without correction. The size of the differences (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 for a good effect at 125 mg in 136 people) limits how much expectation can explain, so one level, not two. The social, empathy, sex-specific and earlier-use findings are worded as weaker and are not rated separately.

inconsistency.note: The direction agrees at Basel, Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco for ratings of drug effect, liking and good effect. Where results differ (closeness higher in San Francisco than in Basel, 'anxious' higher in Chicago, sociability marginal and only at the higher dose, earlier use opposite in Basel), the statement says so and does not rest on them.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes volunteers in laboratory sessions and says where they differ from real life (healthy, screened, mostly new to MDMA, a fixed known amount, a hospital room with researchers present). It does not say why people take it, which none of these papers measured; what people felt in real use comes from one small observational study (Parrott & Lasky, 1998), described with its limits and not part of this rating.

imprecision.note: 166 people for the main ratings, with differences far larger than their spread (SDs of 20 to 33 around averages of 56 to 85, against 3 to 7 on placebo). The smaller samples (16, 9, 32) carry the secondary findings and are described as such; no intervals are printed for the ratings.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: the Basel and three-site papers are pooled analyses by the teams that ran the studies, the three-site pool is not registered, and the registry records of the Basel studies were not read. No sign of selective omission, but unpublished studies cannot be excluded.

rate.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which the laboratory studies did not measure. The real-life sentences rest on one observational study of 45 people with no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, unblinded self-ratings and no spread printed (ROBINS-E very high on its study card); they qualify the claim and are not part of the moderate rating, and on their own would be very low (observational start, risk of bias -2, imprecision -1). Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.
rate.population: Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory); outside the laboratory, 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub: 15 with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, 15 with one to nine and 15 who had never taken it
rate.exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested; outside the laboratory, tablets sold as ecstasy taken by people's own choice at a club, content not tested (study condition, self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group), with alcohol, cannabis or cocaine taken by some in every group
rate.comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people; outside the laboratory, people at the same club who had never taken ecstasy (10 of 15 drank alcohol that night), and each group's own drug-free session before the night
rate.outcome: Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes; outside the laboratory, 16 single-item mood self-ratings (0 to 100) before the night, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later
rate.magnitude: Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses). Outside the laboratory (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; 15 people per group; 0 to 100 self-ratings, means only; Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group): at the club good tempered 85 (comparison), 90 (novice) and 88 (regular); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); 7 days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39). Group by session interactions: p < 0.001 for sad, depressed and abnormal; p < 0.01 for unsociable and unpleasant; p < 0.05 for good tempered.
rate.short: Mostly good: in lab studies, 67 in 100 called it positive afterwards. It lasted about four hours. Many also got a dry mouth or a clenched jaw.
rate.rate: Lab trials where each volunteer got both MDMA and a dummy pill, and the gap was huge; one step below strong for possible bias. The club study alone would rate very low.

risk_of_bias.note: Convenience sample of site clients with the response rate not reported; 72 of 486 (14.8%) excluded for a missing or prefer-not-to-say answer on using alone; one unvalidated item that did not define alone; reasons limited to pre-worded options (the most chosen joins convenience, comfort and home), with two further reasons coded from written answers and not comparable with the options; correlates from a data-driven model in 306 complete cases without allowance for clustering by site (card sc_papamihali_2020; JBI moderate).

indirectness.note: The overdose part rests on coroners' figures cited second-hand, without definitions; the survey did not record overdoses by occasion.

imprecision.note: 414 respondents give about plus or minus 4 points on the main share.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single survey.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low and is rated as a description of the population sampled (clients of harm reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018); rated down for risk of bias and, for the overdose part, indirectness, giving very low. The main finding, that most clients used alone at least sometimes, is unlikely to be reversed by these biases, but the exact share and the order of reasons depend on who was sampled and how the options were worded. The correlates are associations from a selected model. Status single study.
rate.population: Clients of 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites in all five health regions of British Columbia, Canada, May to August 2018: 414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months (62.6% men; 34.3% not regularly housed; past-week use of opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%), recruited by convenience at the sites
rate.exposure: Using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, from one self-report item (share of the time drugs were used alone, in bands, counted as any against none; alone not defined for respondents)
rate.comparator: Respondents who did not use alone in the past 7 days (100), for the correlates; none for the reasons
rate.outcome: Reasons chosen from a short list (more than one allowed, with free text, from which the authors coded two further reasons), asked only of those who used alone; characteristics associated with using alone; self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months
rate.magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): listed options: convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), safer alone 30 (9.6%); coded by the authors from written answers: no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other reasons that could not be coded 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.
rate.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites had used alone at least once in the past week. The top reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
rate.rate: One survey of 414 people who happened to visit harm reduction sites in British Columbia in 2018. Nobody told them what counted as alone, and reasons were picked from a short list.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement: one retrospective lifetime question; impairment items borrowed from meditation research gave counts that do not agree; the lasting-symptom items have no comparison group (card sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: The self-selected survey's higher figure (64 in 100) asked a different question of a different sample; reported as such, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: an opt-in commercial panel matched on three characteristics only, in one country in 2021, called nationally representative by its authors; the share of the panel who had ever used a psychedelic was higher than the authors had expected from national data when they planned the sample (card sc_simonsson_2023, selection effects).

imprecision.note: 613 people; the rarer figures are stated as counts with their denominators.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled: starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low; never upgraded. Status single study: the frequencies come from one survey; the self-selected survey and the prospective cohort are reported as context, not as replication. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication: a signal, not an estimate.
rate.population: Adults in the United States who had ever used a classic psychedelic, in an opt-in online panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity (613 of 2,822), with a self-selected online sample and one prospective cohort for comparison
rate.exposure: Lifetime use of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro)
rate.comparator: None for the frequencies (no group without psychedelic use answered the same questions)
rate.outcome: Challenging, difficult or distressing experiences; impaired functioning and its length; symptoms lasting days that respondents attributed to psychedelics; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others; help-seeking
rate.magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%, slightly to strongly agree). Lithium (8 people) OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34), adjusted only for the other medicines. Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks (any fall) in 85 of the 279 with both measurements (30.5%).
rate.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
rate.rate: One online survey of 613 US adults from a sign-up panel, matched only on sex, age and ethnicity. Two of its questions gave counts that don't agree, and no one who hadn't used psychedelics was asked.

risk_of_bias.note: Blinding not achieved in the trials; self-reported outcomes.

indirectness.note: Not rated down separately: the claim reports the depression estimates as coming from trials mostly in PTSD.

imprecision.note: One small trial per condition; intervals include no effect.

rate.reasoning: The underlying evidence for each condition outside PTSD is one small randomized trial or an uncontrolled study, as found by systematic reviews searched up to October 2023 and March 2024. Starting from randomized trials, rated down once for risk of bias (unblinding) and twice for imprecision, giving very low certainty, which matches the Cochrane rating for MDMA. The claim states insufficient evidence rather than no effect: the point estimates in the life-threatening-illness trial favour MDMA, but the intervals include no effect. Trials published after these searches (read by another reader) are for the editor to join.
rate.population: People with conditions other than PTSD: anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, tinnitus, alcohol use disorder, couples with one partner with PTSD, depressive symptoms
rate.exposure: MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA in one to three sessions with psychotherapy)
rate.comparator: Placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same therapy; none in open-label and uncontrolled studies
rate.outcome: Condition-specific symptoms (anxiety, depression); number and design of the trials available
rate.magnitude: Life-threatening illness (Cochrane, 1 trial, 18): STAI-T −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33), very low certainty. Depressive symptoms (network meta-analysis; MDMA trials mostly PTSD): high-dose MDMA against psychedelic-trial placebo 5.32 HAMD-17 points (2.26 to 8.32); against antidepressant-trial placebo 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78). Studies outside PTSD: randomized, 18, 12 and 13 participants; open-label, 14 (alcohol use disorder); uncontrolled, 6 couples.
rate.short: Nobody can say yet. Outside PTSD, it's been tried for a few things. They include tinnitus, drinking problems, and anxiety in autistic adults or in people who are very ill.
rate.rate: Each condition rests on one tiny trial at most, the largest with 18 people. People could usually tell whether they'd had MDMA, and comparisons didn't run for long.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, some concerns (card sc_pennington_2023): people who failed a manipulation check were left out of that analysis (3.3% to 12%, not given by condition); attitudes reported right after an explicit story are open to demand effects; for the drug-use against health-concern comparison the questionnaire wording also differed (four items named opioids).

inconsistency.note: One study. The authors say two earlier vignette studies agree that drug problems are among the most stigmatized conditions, but as the paper describes them only Rundle et al. (2021) compared a substance use disorder with other conditions; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition. The two disagree on the brain-disease label, partly because they used different measures.

indirectness.note: A young online convenience sample without substance use or psychiatric diagnoses in themselves or close relatives, one hypothetical story, and self-reported attitudes and a pretend money task instead of how people who use drugs are treated; the words tested describe the condition, not the person; the one comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010) used one story about a man under court supervision and attendees of talks on substance use at mental-health conferences, mostly doctoral-level.

imprecision.note: The drug-use contrasts are precise (for example d 0.87, 0.74 to 0.99); the label effects that are inconclusive are stated as such, not as no effect.

publication_bias.note: Registered report accepted before the results; all outcomes reported.

rate.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), now read, adds the comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording, in one story and one sample of conference attendees: allocation by alternation and 29% non-completion give it a high risk of bias (card sc_kelly_2010: RoB 2 high), its small difference (d about 0.2, approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation) relies on an unstated one-sided test, and taken alone it would be rated very low; the displayed rating is set by the pre-registered study. Each contrast rests on one study and neither repeats the other, so the status stays single study. Status single study.
rate.population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized; and 516 attendees of talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008, described by the authors as mental health care providers (mean age 51; 64.5% with doctoral-level degrees; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems; Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
rate.exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor); in the second study, a man in court-ordered treatment described as 'a substance abuser' (against as having 'a substance use disorder')
rate.comparator: Readers assigned to the other wording (at random in the pre-registered study; by alternation of the forms in Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
rate.outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task; agreement with a mixed set of blame, punishment, expected-violence and non-medical statements, willingness for social contact, and treatment and biological-cause statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
rate.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), label version vs 'substance use disorder' version: 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58) on a 1–6 scale, t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed as .02 (one-sided by the editors' calculation; two-sided about .041), d printed as 0.20 (about 0.17 to 0.18 recomputed; approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation); 'social threat' (willingness for social contact) and 'victim-treatment' (treatment, genetic and chemical-imbalance causes, severity) subscales, no difference (ps > .59).
rate.short: Yes, some do. People judged a person more harshly when their troubles were said to come from drug use, not a health concern.
rate.rate: A fair test: chance decided which story each of 1,613 online volunteers read. But readers gave their views after one made-up story, and many were young.

lines.statement: In healthy, screened adults given MDMA by mouth by researchers in laboratories, and a placebo on another day, MDMA raised ratings of the drug's effect, of a good effect and of feeling happy, and, in one study, of feeling open and close to others, and also raised ratings of a bad effect and of physical complaints, in the same sessions (five papers from Basel, Chicago, San Francisco and Zurich, not fully independent: the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers a senior author, and one author is on four of the five). In 166 volunteers aged 18 to 45 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel, four in five new to MDMA, the average highest self-rating of 'any drug effect' on a 0 to 100 line was 73 in men and 85 in women after 125 mg (136 people), against 4 on placebo, and lower after 75 mg (30 other people); of 'good drug effect' it was 77 and 82 after 125 mg, against 3 or 4. Four of the 166 reported no effect. The effect began on average 33 minutes after the dose (SD 24), peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2); in 16 volunteers in Zurich it began 20 to 120 minutes after the dose and lasted about 3 hours. In a 32-person Basel study (probably within the 166), ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (F(1,31) 121, 81 and 68; p < 0.001), as did scores for well-being, extroversion and activity, with no rise in anxiety; in Zurich, positive mood averaged 40% of the highest possible score against 0.6% on placebo and thought disorder 25% against 0, with no rise in aggression-anger, apprehension-anxiety or depressiveness. The social effects are less settled: a 'sociable' rating rose at 1.5 mg/kg in 9 people in Chicago (+19.7 points against -6.3; p = .04, which the authors call marginal) while a friendliness scale did not change significantly; closeness was rated higher in San Francisco than in Basel; peak ratings of drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ significantly between three sites (220 volunteers, partly overlapping the others; no means printed, and no significant difference is not proof of equality); and empathy and money-sharing tests rose in one Basel study, in men only on post hoc tests. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. 'Bad drug effect' averaged 13 in men and 24 in women after 125 mg against 2 on placebo, higher in women also after allowing for dose per kilogram and blood level (SDs of 22 and 24, so ratings varied widely). In the first 6 hours, MDMA against placebo in 166 people: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41% and jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), against 0 to 6%; at 24 hours, lack of appetite 31% (1% on placebo), lack of energy 30% (3%) and headache 33% (15%). Nine people reported anxiety, all after 125 mg; the authors say verbal support reduced it and no benzodiazepine was used. The paper reports no serious adverse event, depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg in the next one to two weeks, and 'flashbacks' (not defined) in 9%, 8 to 50 hours after the dose. Asked at the end of the study, 67% of 141 volunteers called the experience positive, 18% neutral and 15% disappointing or bad; 19% would probably not take MDMA again, 47% only in another controlled study and 34% perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known. Why people take MDMA was not studied: none of the five laboratory papers asked people who use ecstasy why they do or what they feel in real use (one small study outside the laboratory, below, measured what they felt); two say, citing other papers, that sociability and empathy are reasons for recreational use. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show a start that ranged up to 120 minutes in Zurich; a lowering of Zurich ratings by about 60% by an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion before MDMA; peak blood levels averaging 1.29 times higher in women than in men at the same 125 mg; and, in Chicago and less clearly San Francisco, a lower 'any drug effect' rating with more earlier MDMA use (not for other ratings, and the other way round in Basel); a pill of different content was not tested, as every capsule held a known amount. No one took a second dose within a session, so what happens when people take more was not measured here (controlled second-dose studies are covered in a separate claim). The sessions differ from real life: healthy, screened volunteers (mostly new to MDMA in Basel and Zurich; earlier use in Chicago and San Francisco) took a known capsule and nothing else, at an amount set by the researchers, in a hospital or laboratory room (22.7 degrees Celsius in Basel) with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco; in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis people were alone and gave higher 'anxious' ratings than at the other sites, which the authors suggest, untested, may reflect company. The end-of-study answers came from people given MDMA by researchers, not from people who chose it, and heat, crowds and other drugs were not part of the MDMA sessions. Outside the laboratory, one small study with no placebo followed 45 people aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub, from a drug-free session before a Saturday night out to the club and then 2 and 7 days later: 30 who had used ecstasy before (15 of them ten or more times) took tablets of untested content by their own choice that night, and 15 who had never taken it, 10 of whom drank alcohol, went to the same club (Parrott & Lasky, 1998). At the club all three groups rated their mood as good and the ecstasy groups' ratings were not clearly better (sad 9 against 20 out of 100, p < 0.10; good tempered about the same), though they felt more 'abnormal'; the authors had expected better moods and point to the setting and expectation, the comparison group's drinking, ratings already near the top of the scale and a mood list with no items on elation or empathy. Two days later both ecstasy groups rated themselves sadder (56 and 53 against 22), more unsociable and more 'abnormal', and the novice group also more depressed, more unpleasant and less good tempered (in the regular group these three reached only p < 0.10); seven days later the groups rated these moods alike again. These are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, with means only, many comparisons and no correction, and sleep and drug use after the night were not recorded, so the study shows what this group reported over that week, not what MDMA alone did.
lines.population: Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory); outside the laboratory, 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub: 15 with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, 15 with one to nine and 15 who had never taken it
lines.exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested; outside the laboratory, tablets sold as ecstasy taken by people's own choice at a club, content not tested (study condition, self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group), with alcohol, cannabis or cocaine taken by some in every group
lines.comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people; outside the laboratory, people at the same club who had never taken ecstasy (10 of 15 drank alcohol that night), and each group's own drug-free session before the night
lines.outcome: Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes; outside the laboratory, 16 single-item mood self-ratings (0 to 100) before the night, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later
lines.magnitude: Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses). Outside the laboratory (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; 15 people per group; 0 to 100 self-ratings, means only; Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group): at the club good tempered 85 (comparison), 90 (novice) and 88 (regular); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); 7 days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39). Group by session interactions: p < 0.001 for sad, depressed and abnormal; p < 0.01 for unsociable and unpleasant; p < 0.05 for good tempered.
lines.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which the laboratory studies did not measure. The real-life sentences rest on one observational study of 45 people with no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, unblinded self-ratings and no spread printed (ROBINS-E very high on its study card); they qualify the claim and are not part of the moderate rating, and on their own would be very low (observational start, risk of bias -2, imprecision -1). Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.

lines.short: Mostly good: in lab studies, 67 in 100 called it positive afterwards. It lasted about four hours. Many also got a dry mouth or a clenched jaw.
lines.but: These were healthy volunteers in a lab, given a known pill and nothing else. The one club study was small, with no dummy pill.
how: In Basel labs, 136 healthy adults rated the good feeling about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 on a dummy pill. In a study of 32, people felt more open and closer to others.
Unwanted effects came too: 55 in 100 had a dry mouth and 40 in 100 of those asked clenched their jaw. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive, 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.
It began in about half an hour on average and lasted about four hours. For some the start was slow; an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that wasn't tested.
At a London club, people who took ecstasy weren't clearly happier than other clubbers. Two days later they felt sadder, but not a week later. Pills were untested, so MDMA's part is unclear.

lines.statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release (counted from day 2), and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate over the whole follow-up was 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625 to 831). The analyses by time since release used the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day (New Zealand's only cohort and one from Washington State could not): the rate was 1,612 (1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release, and the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because, by the authors' reading of their data, deaths in custody may have been recorded in some cohorts as deaths on the day of release, probably inflating the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years; 826, with an interval of 0 to 3,455, in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024; the paper does not say whether counted from the first release in the study period or from the latest one), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers, and the paper reports no check of how deaths were certified or coded across countries and decades; and it analysed only age and sex, with no information on what happened between release and death, so it says nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance and cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People released from incarceration (prison or jail) in 18 cohorts of everyone released in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018 (1,471,526 people; 88.3% men); analyses by time since release in the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day
lines.exposure: Time since release (days 2–7, week 2, weeks 3–4, weeks 9–12, more than a year)
lines.comparator: Later periods after release in the same cohorts (no comparison with the general population)
lines.outcome: Crude death rates per 100,000 person-years, all causes and by underlying cause coded in death registers (alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional or undetermined intent; suicide; cardiovascular disease)
lines.magnitude: Borschmann et al. (2024), pooled crude rates per 100,000 person-years: all causes, whole follow-up 725 (95% CI 625–831), 18 cohorts; days 2–7 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%, and more than 1 year 737 (636–844), from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day, as are all the period-specific figures below; first week vs week 2 IRR 1.5 (1.2–1.8), vs weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), vs weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0). Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug poisoning 657 (332–1076), suicide 135 (36–277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: poisoning 146 (103–197), 16,126 of 75,427 deaths (21.4%); 14,671 of the 16,126 (91.0%) more than 4 weeks after release (from which release is not stated). Release day 4036 (887–8940), 826 (0–3455) in the ten cohorts that separated deaths in custody. Cohorts 236 to 1183; days 2–7 Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). Excluding time back in custody (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. The rates by time since release come from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (Figure 2), which the statement says and which does not change the rating. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.

lines.q: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?
lines.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
lines.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.

lines.statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Clients of 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites in all five health regions of British Columbia, Canada, May to August 2018: 414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months (62.6% men; 34.3% not regularly housed; past-week use of opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%), recruited by convenience at the sites
lines.exposure: Using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, from one self-report item (share of the time drugs were used alone, in bands, counted as any against none; alone not defined for respondents)
lines.comparator: Respondents who did not use alone in the past 7 days (100), for the correlates; none for the reasons
lines.outcome: Reasons chosen from a short list (more than one allowed, with free text, from which the authors coded two further reasons), asked only of those who used alone; characteristics associated with using alone; self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months
lines.magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): listed options: convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), safer alone 30 (9.6%); coded by the authors from written answers: no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other reasons that could not be coded 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low and is rated as a description of the population sampled (clients of harm reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018); rated down for risk of bias and, for the overdose part, indirectness, giving very low. The main finding, that most clients used alone at least sometimes, is unlikely to be reversed by these biases, but the exact share and the order of reasons depend on who was sampled and how the options were worded. The correlates are associations from a selected model. Status single study.

lines.q: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?
lines.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites had used alone at least once in the past week. The top reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
lines.but: It was one survey in one part of Canada. Everyone asked already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, did a short survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.
