lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session for nine of the ten (one chose none), the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), the text reports 16 trials playing a set playlist through headphones, although Table 3 describes one of those trials with stereo speakers; one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
lines.exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions: one standard playlist (with one exception), as patients described it a week later; a Western classical or an overtone-based playlist, in randomized order within each person; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
lines.comparator: No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
lines.outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; mystical-type experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) self-rated after each session; smoking abstinence by chosen playlist; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
lines.magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613. Strickland et al. (2021), n = 10, randomized sessions 1 and 2: MEQ30 0.68 (SD 0.20) overtone against 0.52 (SD 0.21) Western classical, dz 0.57, p = 0.107 (dose-adjusted b = 0.14, p = 0.108); editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36 (dz about −0.12 to 1.23); CEQ 0.33 (SD 0.20) against 0.34 (SD 0.22), dz −0.11, p = 0.74 (editors' dz interval about −0.73 to 0.51). Abstinence by chosen playlist, not randomized: 5 of 6 (overtone) against 2 of 4 (classical) at the end of treatment and 4 of 6 against 2 of 4 at long-term follow-up (editors' Fisher p = 0.50 and 1.0).
lines.reasoning: Rated from the one randomized comparison, the best evidence on whether the music itself changes a session: randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The correlational evidence on how patients experienced the music (Kaelen et al., 2018) is very low on its own, as before (low, minus two for risk of bias and one for imprecision). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of the music nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status single study: each question rests on one small study (two genres compared in 10 people; the music experience and the fall in depression in 19 patients); the panel survey adds only null associations, one very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found none that compared settings, music included; trials treating substance use were outside its scope. The published correction to Strickland et al. (2021; doi 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119), read on 12 November 2026, changes only the acknowledgments, so no figure here is affected. The only comparison with a no-music condition in psychedelic sessions that these sources mention, a 1970 quasi-randomized study of LSD sessions (Gaston and Eagle), is known only from Strickland et al.'s description and has not been read. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card.

lines.q: Does music change how a trip goes?
lines.short: Nobody knows for sure: no study we read compared music with silence. 18 of 19 patients said music helped at times; 10 said it sometimes made things harder.
lines.but: The one test that compared two playlists had just 10 people, so it could easily miss a difference.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.
Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest time to the music did not rate it as harder than others did.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does music change how a psychedelic session goes?

lines.statement: In an online panel of US adults matched to the population on sex, age and ethnicity only (Prolific, October 2021; Simonsson et al., 2023), 613 of 2,822 respondents (21.7%) had ever used a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote or San Pedro). Asked once, looking back over their whole life, 362 of the 613 (59.1%) said they had never had a challenging, difficult or distressing experience with them, 143 (23.3%) rarely, 80 (13.1%) occasionally and 28 (4.6%) regularly or frequently: 41 in 100 at least once (editors' calculation). 28 (4.6%) said their ability to function had been severely impaired, and 55 (9.0%; printed 8.9%) that impairment had lasted more than a day, 21 of them (3.4%) more than a month (editors' sum), but the two impairment questions gave counts that do not agree (176 reported some impairment, 262 gave its length). All 613, including the 362 who said they had never had one, were asked about their most challenging experience; in the days or weeks after it, 41 (6.7%) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others, including 9 (1.5%) attempts to harm themselves, and 16 (2.6%) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological help. 350 (57.1%) reported at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they put down to psychedelics, most often feeling anxious (36.1%) or difficulty sleeping (27.9%), but these questions, borrowed from meditation research, were not asked of people who had not used psychedelics or about times without them, so how many such symptoms would have happened anyway is unknown; 482 (78.6%) agreed, at least slightly, that they were glad to have used psychedelics. Challenging experiences were linked most often to LSD (by 31.5% of those who had used it, against 19.7% for psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT and 14.7% for mescaline, peyote or San Pedro), but how often each drug had been used was not asked. The 8 people taking lithium and the 16 taking another mood stabilizer at the time of their most challenging experience had higher odds of later harm thoughts or attempts (odds ratios 22.34, 95% CI 1.78 to 279.65, and 5.84, 1.40 to 24.34, adjusted only for the other medicines), estimates too imprecise, and too open to confounding by the conditions these medicines treat, to give a risk. In a self-selected online sample of people who had used psychedelics, 555 of 869 (64 in 100) said the experience they described had included a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort (Wood et al., 2024), a reminder that such figures depend on who is asked and how. In a prospective study that measured well-being before and after a planned psychedelic experience (Haijen et al., 2018), 85 of the 279 people who answered both surveys (30 in 100, editors' calculation) scored lower two weeks later, counting any fall however small, and they had not rated the experience as more challenging than the others (the paper gives no statistics for this comparison); many who started did not answer the later surveys, and with no comparison group the fall cannot be put down to the drug. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Adults in the United States who had ever used a classic psychedelic, in an opt-in online panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity (613 of 2,822), with a self-selected online sample and one prospective cohort for comparison
lines.exposure: Lifetime use of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro)
lines.comparator: None for the frequencies (no group without psychedelic use answered the same questions)
lines.outcome: Challenging, difficult or distressing experiences; impaired functioning and its length; symptoms lasting days that respondents attributed to psychedelics; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others; help-seeking
lines.magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%, slightly to strongly agree). Lithium (8 people) OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34), adjusted only for the other medicines. Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks (any fall) in 85 of the 279 with both measurements (30.5%).
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled: starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low; never upgraded. Status single study: the frequencies come from one survey; the self-selected survey and the prospective cohort are reported as context, not as replication. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication: a signal, not an estimate.

lines.q: How common are bad trips, and can problems last?
lines.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
lines.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 had thoughts of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.
57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But nobody who hadn't used them was asked.
lines.q_on_site_now: How often are psychedelic trips difficult, and can problems last?

lines.statement: In nine healthy volunteers in Germany (aged 25 to 48; 2 women and 7 men; how they were recruited or screened is not reported), eating pieces of a poppy-seed cake once (study conditions: 12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds per person, eaten over 10 to 120 minutes), made with the one seed batch, of eight poppy-seed products bought in German supermarkets, health-food shops and a bakery, that held by far the most morphine (151.6 µg per gram of seeds, about 18 to 250 times the 0.6 to 8.4 µg/g of the other seven, editors' arithmetic; a second package of the batch was comparable, other batches of the same maker held 1.1 µg/g), with no control cake and no urine sample from before eating reported, was followed in every volunteer by urinary morphine above 1 µg/mL, the limit for sport that the International Olympic Committee added to its medical code in 1998, measured by GC-MS (Thevis et al., 2003, published as a case report from the Institute of Biochemistry of the German Sport University Cologne; financial support from the Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft, Bonn). Every volunteer was above the limit in at least 2 urine samples (51 of 80 samples, 2 to 8 per person, editors' count), with peaks of 1.93 to 10.04 µg/mL 4 to 11 hours after eating; values above 4 µg/mL, the highest included, were estimated from the calibration curve because such values had not been expected. In eight volunteers the last sample above the limit came 10.25 to 24 hours after eating and the final samples, at 43.75 to 48 hours, held 0.20 to 0.36 µg/mL; one volunteer, whose peak was the highest, was still above the limit at 47.5 hours (1.21 µg/mL), a result the authors concede was shown in only one person after a high amount. All eight products contained morphine and codeine, with codeine negligible in all; urinary codeine was 0.06 to 0.82 µg/mL. The paper judged results only against this sports limit, by GC-MS, without immunoassay screening and without workplace cut-offs, so it cannot show what a workplace drug test would report, and the editors do not apply cut-offs the paper did not use. The morphine each person ate is printed differently in the two tables for every volunteer (1.6 to 6.8 mg in one, 1.8 to 7.7 mg in the other), the cake itself was not analysed, urine dilution was not reported, and the final sample the text dates at 46 to 48 hours appears in the table at 43.75 to 48 hours. A positive here is a urine result, morphine above a limit; effects were not measured. Thebaine, another poppy alkaloid that the authors cite another study as finding in urine after poppy seeds but not after morphine, codeine or street heroin, was not measured, so these results cannot tell poppy seeds apart from heroin or morphine use. The batch was chosen for its unusually high morphine, so the results describe a high-end exposure, not typical poppy-seed foods; the authors' advice that athletes avoid poppy-seed foods before and during competitions goes beyond the data and is not adopted. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Nine healthy volunteers in Germany, aged 25 to 48 (2 women, 62 and 68 kg; 7 men, 67 to 88 kg); recruitment, screening for opioid or codeine medicines and other poppy-seed foods, and ethics approval not reported
lines.exposure: Poppy-seed cake made with the seed batch holding 151.6 µg of morphine per gram (the highest of eight products bought in Germany; the other seven 0.6 to 8.4 µg/g), eaten once (study conditions: 12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds per person, over 10 to 120 minutes; morphine eaten printed as 1.6 to 6.8 mg in Table II and as 1.8 to 7.7 mg in Table III)
lines.comparator: None: no control cake, no unexposed group and no urine sample from before eating reported; only the course over time within each person
lines.outcome: Total urinary morphine by GC-MS after enzymatic hydrolysis, in urine collected for 24 hours and a final sample at 43.75 to 48 hours, judged against the 1 µg/mL limit of the International Olympic Committee; urinary codeine as a range; morphine content of eight poppy-seed products
lines.magnitude: Thevis et al. (2003), 9 volunteers, 80 urine samples: above 1 µg/mL in 9 of 9 volunteers (Wilson 95% interval 70.1% to 100%, editors' calculation) and in 51 of 80 samples (2 to 8 per volunteer; editors' count); peaks 1.93 to 10.04 µg/mL at 4 to 11 hours (13 values above 4 µg/mL, from 5 volunteers, estimated from the calibration curve); last sample above 1 µg/mL at 10.25 to 24.00 hours in 8 volunteers and at 47.50 hours in 1 (1.21 µg/mL; 1 of 9, 2.0% to 43.5%); final samples of the other 8 at 43.75 to 48.00 hours, 0.20 to 0.36 µg/mL; urinary codeine 0.06 to 0.82 µg/mL. Morphine in the eight products 8.4, 6.9, 151.6, 2.1, 4.1, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.6 µg/g (the batch used about 18 to 250 times the others, editors' arithmetic). Morphine eaten: 1.6 to 6.8 mg in Table II, 1.8 to 7.7 mg in Table III; seeds eaten times 151.6 µg/g gives 1.90 to 7.93 mg (editors' arithmetic). Peaks did not rise steadily with seeds eaten (52.3 g, peak 5.88 µg/mL; 38.1 g, peak 10.04 µg/mL). No comparison condition, so no difference can be given.
lines.reasoning: An uncontrolled excretion study in nine volunteers starts low, as a description of what happened after eating this cake (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 (no control and no sample from before eating; unvalidated method with estimated high values; no dilution adjustment; two tables disagreeing on the morphine eaten), indirectness −1 (one unusually morphine-rich batch; a sports limit only) and imprecision −1 (nine people) bring it to very low, the floor. Worded as 'describes', because it reports concentrations after one exposure without a comparison. The paper uses only the sports limit of the time (1 µg/mL, IOC) and GC-MS; it gives no workplace cut-off and no immunoassay result, and the editors do not apply workplace cut-offs the paper does not use. The morphine eaten is given as the range of both tables; the seeds eaten, printed once and consistently, are the study conditions. The authors' general statement about products containing poppy seeds and their advice to athletes are not adopted, because the batch was the most morphine-rich of eight. Thebaine, which the authors cite from another study as a marker of poppy seeds, was not measured, so nothing here tells poppy seeds from heroin or morphine use. Status single study: the authors cite earlier reports of comparable seed contents and urine concentrations, not read here. Funding: the Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.

lines.q: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?
lines.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
lines.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested. It had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.
lines.q_on_site_now: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?

lines.statement: In laboratory tests of the first commercial nitazene test strip (BTNX Rapid Response; maker's cut-off 2000 ng/mL isotonitazene) on pure nitazene standards in water and on nearly pure powders from drug-market monitoring, compared with known content, the strips detected most nitazenes tested but missed six of the seven desnitazenes tested and three other analogues. Read from photographs by two blinded raters and by image analysis, isotonitazene read positive in all six replicates from 3000 ng/mL with one lot and 2000 ng/mL with another, obtained about four months apart. With one lot and one strip per concentration, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues read positive at 9000 ng/mL or less; nine did not at 9000 ng/mL: six desnitazenes, which lack the 5-nitro group (among them metodesnitazene and etodesnitazene), 5-aminoisotonitazene and two analogues with a longer link between the rings; the seventh desnitazene tested, 5-methyl etodesnitazene, was detected. Six powders obtained in Belgian drug-market monitoring, each estimated as more than 90% one nitazene, all read positive at about 1 and 0.1 mg/mL (6 of 6; editors' Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%) (De Vrieze et al., 2024). In a second laboratory, the strips detected metonitazene from 1 µg/mL and N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene from 5 µg/mL (ten strips per level), and reacted to none of 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds at two concentrations (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). No study read tested nitazene-free street samples or mixtures in which a nitazene is a small part of heroin, other opioids or stimulants, so how often the strips miss nitazenes or give false positives in real samples is unknown; preliminary street-sample figures cited from the maker's material (12 samples) are unpublished. The first study's authors write that a negative result does not mean a sample is free of nitazenes or safe, and that a positive one does not show which nitazene is present or how much. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Nitazene reference standards in water (33 analogues in one laboratory, three in another), six nearly pure nitazene powders from Belgian drug-market monitoring, and 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds
lines.exposure: BTNX Rapid Response nitazene test strips (two lots), read from photographs by two blinded raters and by image analysis, or by laboratory staff
lines.comparator: Known content of prepared solutions; LC-QTOF-MS identification of the main compound in each powder
lines.outcome: Lowest isotonitazene concentration detected, which analogues read positive, readings of the powders, and reactions to other compounds
lines.magnitude: De Vrieze et al.: isotonitazene limit (all six replicates positive) 3000 ng/mL (lot A) and 2000 ng/mL (lot B), the same by visual and image-analysis scoring; analogues (lot B, single strips) 24 of 33 positive at 9000 ng/mL or less (visually 16 at 1000 and 3000 ng/mL, 7 at 3000 ng/mL only, 1 at 9000 ng/mL only, by the text), 9 not detected at 9000 ng/mL (six of seven desnitazenes, 5-aminoisotonitazene, two ethylene-linker analogues); powders 6 of 6 positive at both concentrations (Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%, editors' calculation on the card). Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024): limits 1 µg/mL (metonitazene) and 5 µg/mL (N-piperidinyl etonitazene, protonitazene); no reaction with 76 non-nitazene compounds at 0.01 and 0.5 or 1 mg/mL.
lines.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision gives very low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of nitazenes by one brand of strip. Status replicated: two independent laboratories (Ghent University; NIST) found detection at µg/mL concentrations. The preliminary street-sample figures are second-hand from the maker's material and not counted.

lines.short: Mostly, in the lab. They picked up 24 of 33 kinds of nitazene but missed most desnitazenes, so a negative doesn't rule nitazenes out.
lines.but: Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested. Mixed street drugs were not.
how: One lab tried 33 kinds of nitazene. The strips picked up 24. They missed 6 of the 7 desnitazenes, even at high strength.
Six nearly pure powders from the drug market all showed up.
A second lab found the strips did not react to 76 other drugs and cutting agents.
No study we read tested street drugs where a nitazene is a small part of a mix. So how often strips get it wrong on real samples is unknown.

lines.statement: For conditions other than PTSD, evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy helps. The systematic reviews read here (searches up to March 2024) found only small studies outside PTSD: one randomized trial each in anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (18 people), social anxiety in autistic adults (12) and tinnitus (13), an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (14), an uncontrolled study of couples in which one partner has PTSD (6 couples) and a Swiss case series. The Cochrane review rated the evidence in life-threatening illness very uncertain: in its one trial, MDMA against placebo changed trait anxiety by −14.7 points on a 20 to 80 scale (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and depression by −6.3 points on a 0 to 63 scale (−16.93 to 4.33). A network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials were mostly in PTSD, found high-dose MDMA better than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials by 5.3 HAMD-17 points (95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32) but not clearly better than the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5, −2.79 to 5.78), a comparison made only indirectly. A critical narrative review found that, for MDMA, only the two phase 3 PTSD trials met its minimum standard (randomized, more than 15 people per group) and called MDMA for PTSD a signal needing replication. The reviews report that blinding was rarely achieved and that controlled follow-up was short. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (one trial per condition outside PTSD).
lines.population: People with conditions other than PTSD: anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, tinnitus, alcohol use disorder, couples with one partner with PTSD, depressive symptoms
lines.exposure: MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA in one to three sessions with psychotherapy)
lines.comparator: Placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same therapy; none in open-label and uncontrolled studies
lines.outcome: Condition-specific symptoms (anxiety, depression); number and design of the trials available
lines.magnitude: Life-threatening illness (Cochrane, 1 trial, 18): STAI-T −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33), very low certainty. Depressive symptoms (network meta-analysis; MDMA trials mostly PTSD): high-dose MDMA against psychedelic-trial placebo 5.32 HAMD-17 points (2.26 to 8.32); against antidepressant-trial placebo 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78). Studies outside PTSD: randomized, 18, 12 and 13 participants; open-label, 14 (alcohol use disorder); uncontrolled, 6 couples.
lines.reasoning: The underlying evidence for each condition outside PTSD is one small randomized trial or an uncontrolled study, as found by systematic reviews searched up to October 2023 and March 2024. Starting from randomized trials, rated down once for risk of bias (unblinding) and twice for imprecision, giving very low certainty, which matches the Cochrane rating for MDMA. The claim states insufficient evidence rather than no effect: the point estimates in the life-threatening-illness trial favour MDMA, but the intervals include no effect. Trials published after these searches (read by another reader) are for the editor to join.

lines.q: Can MDMA therapy help with anything besides PTSD?
lines.short: Nobody can say yet. Outside PTSD, it's been tried for a few things. They include tinnitus, drinking problems, and anxiety in autistic adults or in people who are very ill.
lines.but: Each had one tiny trial at most, the biggest with 18 people. And people could usually tell if they'd had MDMA.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found one trial each. There were 18 people anxious about a serious illness, 12 autistic adults with social anxiety, and 13 people with tinnitus.
A study of 14 people with alcohol problems, and one of 6 couples, had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found only the two later PTSD trials were randomized with over 15 people per group. It called even those results a signal needing repeating.
lines.q_on_site_now: What else has MDMA therapy been tried for?

lines.statement: In adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials, all off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing, one dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg, with preparation sessions beforehand, a supervised session of 6 to 10 hours with two therapists or facilitators, and integration sessions afterwards) compared with the same support and a 1-mg dose of psilocybin or a capsule of niacin is associated with larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 and 6 weeks later. In 233 adults with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode) at 22 sites in Europe and North America, 2019 to 2021, the MADRS (0 to 60) fell by 12.0 points after 25 mg, 7.9 after 10 mg and 5.4 after 1 mg by week 3, the primary end point: a difference of −6.6 points for 25 mg against 1 mg (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9), while 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg (−2.5, −6.2 to 1.2; P = 0.18) (Goodwin et al., 2022). Because the 10-mg comparison failed, the prespecified testing order stopped, so every secondary result, including those for 25 mg, counts formally as not significant: at week 3, 29 of 79 given 25 mg (37 in 100) and 14 of 79 given 1 mg (18 in 100) had responded (a fall of half or more), and 23 of 79 (29 in 100) and 6 of 79 (8 in 100) were in remission; a response kept from week 3 through week 12 was seen in 16 of 79 (20 in 100) against 8 of 79 (10 in 100) (odds ratio 2.2, 0.9 to 5.4). Between weeks 3 and 12, 26 of the 79 given 25 mg (33 in 100) started another treatment for depression, as did 16 of 79 given 1 mg. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation or self-injury from day 2 to week 3 occurred in 4 of 79 given 25 mg, 3 of 75 given 10 mg (besides 1 hospitalization for severe depression) and none of 79 given 1 mg; after week 3, suicidal behaviour in 3 given 25 mg (all with earlier suicidal behaviour or self-injury and no response at week 3), self-injury or suicidal ideation in 2 given 10 mg and self-injury in 1 given 1 mg (counts by period; the number of distinct people over the 12 weeks is not given). The trial was designed and funded by COMPASS Pathfinder, the company whose proprietary psilocybin formulation was tested, which also did the interpretation and post hoc analyses; 8 of the 74 authors are listed with the company, and the authors' disclosure forms are not printed in the article. In 104 adults with major depression (a current episode of at least 60 days; 13 of 104 met the trial's definition of treatment resistance) at 11 US sites, 2019 to 2022, scores fell by 19.1 points after psilocybin and 6.8 after niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical capsules, by day 43, the primary end point: a difference of −12.3 points (95% CI −17.5 to −7.2), with −12.0 by day 8 and no difference at day 2 (−0.1) (Raison et al., 2023; version corrected on 26 January 2024). Among those assessed at every visit, 20 of 48 assigned to psilocybin (42 in 100) and 5 of 44 assigned to niacin (11 in 100) kept a fall of half or more from day 8 to day 43, which the authors call a sustained response; sustained remission did not differ significantly (12 of 48 against 4 of 44; P = .05). By 6 weeks, 1 of 51 assigned to psilocybin and 9 of 53 assigned to niacin had withdrawn or been lost to follow-up. The authors call the reduction clinically significant, but no threshold for a meaningful difference was set in advance (they argue it afterwards from published values, using the point estimate; the interval reaches 7.2 points, below the 9 points they cite), 'sustained' means through day 43, and they state that the trial cannot show whether the effect would have faded later. No serious adverse events followed dosing and no suicidal or self-injurious behaviour was recorded; from the dosing day through day 9, adverse events judged related to the drug affected 41 of 50 given psilocybin (82 in 100) and 24 of 54 given niacin (44 in 100), and severe related events 4 of 50 and none. Some relative incidences and intervals printed for these adverse events do not fit their counts, so the counts are used (Raison et al., 2023). That trial was sponsored and funded by the Usona Institute, a non-profit medical research organization that supplied the psilocybin, designed the trial, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript; 8 of the 35 authors are listed at the institute, and many authors report fees, grants or shares from companies developing psychedelic and other medicines. Neither trial checked whether participants could tell which they had received; both sets of authors say the acute effects of psilocybin probably weakened the blinding, and the Raison authors say this may have contributed to the effect and to the higher dropout with niacin. A two-page viewpoint on the Goodwin trial, with no data of its own, by an author of the Raison trial report who was not part of the Goodwin team (Gukasyan, 2023), singles out the missing blinding check as perhaps that trial's most serious flaw and argues that the suicidal behaviour of three participants given 25 mg, all with no response at week 3 and earlier suicide attempts or self-injury, should be taken seriously; events coded as suicidal behaviour were indeed all in the 25-mg group, but, as the trial's abstract states, suicidal ideation, behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, serious events included (counted above). The MADRS was rated by remote raters who did not know the group, from participants' own answers. Neither trial compared psilocybin with an established treatment or with an inert placebo; both excluded people judged to be at current risk of suicide and people with psychotic depression (Raison: any personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania), and most participants were White. These results describe psilocybin given in a medical trial with screening and psychological support, not use outside such settings. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials: 233 outpatients with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode; episodes without psychotic features; mean age 39.8; 121 women; 215 White; 14 had used psilocybin before; mean baseline MADRS 32.5) at 22 sites in 10 countries in Europe and North America, March 2019 to September 2021 (Goodwin et al., 2022); and 104 medically healthy adults aged 21 to 65 with major depressive disorder (current episode of at least 60 days; central-rater MADRS of 28 or more at screening; 13 meeting the trial's definition of treatment resistance; median one earlier medicine in the current episode; mean age 41.1; 52 women; 89% White; mean baseline MADRS 35.5 and 35.0) at 11 US sites, December 2019 to June 2022 (Raison et al., 2023). All were off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing. Goodwin excluded people judged to be at clinically significant risk of suicide; Raison excluded active suicidal ideation with intent or plan, suicidal behaviour in the past 12 months, a personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania, moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder, and any psychedelic use in the past 5 years or more than 10 lifetime uses.
lines.exposure: One dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg of the proprietary synthetic formulation COMP360 in Goodwin et al., where 10 mg was also tested; 25 mg of synthetic psilocybin by mouth in Raison et al.), after preparation sessions (at least three therapist meetings; 6 to 8 hours with two facilitators), in a supervised session of 6 to 8 hours with two therapists (Goodwin) or 7 to 10 hours with two facilitators (Raison), followed by integration sessions
lines.comparator: The same preparation, session and integration with a 1-mg dose of the same psilocybin formulation (Goodwin et al., 2022) or with 100 mg of niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical-looking capsules (Raison et al., 2023); no inert placebo and no established treatment
lines.outcome: Clinician-rated depression on the MADRS (0 to 60), rated by telephone by remote raters who did not know the group: change from baseline to week 3 (Goodwin, primary) and to day 43 (Raison, primary); response, remission and sustained response; dropout and starting other treatment; adverse events, including serious events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour
lines.magnitude: Goodwin et al. (2022), modified intention-to-treat (79, 75, 79): MADRS least-squares mean change to week 3 −12.0 (95% CI −14.6 to −9.3) with 25 mg, −7.9 (−10.6 to −5.2) with 10 mg, −5.4 (−8.1 to −2.7) with 1 mg; difference 25 mg against 1 mg −6.6 (−10.2 to −2.9), P<0.001; 10 mg against 1 mg −2.5 (−6.2 to 1.2), P = 0.18. Secondary, formally not significant because hierarchical testing stopped: response at week 3 29/79 (37%) against 14/79 (18%), odds ratio 2.9 (1.2 to 6.6); remission 23/79 (29%) against 6/79 (8%), 4.8 (1.8 to 12.8); sustained response to week 12 16/79 (20%) against 8/79 (10%), 2.2 (0.9 to 5.4). Editors' calculation (Wald): response difference 19.0 percentage points (5.4 to 32.5); remission 21.5 (9.9 to 33.1); sustained response 10.1 (−1.0 to 21.2); standardized difference for the primary contrast about 0.55 (SD about 11.9, back-calculated from the SE of the difference, 1.9). New depression treatment from week 3 to week 12: 26/79 (33%), 18/75 (24%), 16/79 (20%); before week 3: 4/79, 9/75, 14/79. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour: day 2 to week 3, 4/79, 3/75, 0/79; after week 3, 3/79, 2/75, 1/79 (by period). Raison et al. (2023), intention to treat (51, 53): MADRS change to day 43 −19.1 (−22.7 to −15.5) against −6.8 (−10.5 to −3.1), difference −12.3 (−17.5 to −7.2), P<.001; day 8 −12.0 (−16.6 to −7.4), P<.001; day 2 −0.1 (−2.1 to 1.9). Sustained response 20/48 (41.7%) against 5/44 (11.4%), difference 30.3 percentage points (13.5 to 47.1), odds ratio 5.60 (1.87 to 16.74), P = .002; sustained remission 12/48 (25.0%) against 4/44 (9.1%), odds ratio 3.37 (0.99 to 11.47), P = .05. Withdrawn or lost by week 6: 1/51 against 9/53. Related adverse events from dosing to day 9: 41/50 (82%) against 24/54 (44%); severe related 4/50 against 0/54; no serious adverse events after dosing. Editors' calculation: standardized difference at day 43 about 1.0 (SD about 12.7, back-calculated from the interval with 50 and 44 assessed).
lines.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down two levels for risk of bias (participants could very probably tell psilocybin from the control, which neither trial checked, with an outcome that rests on their own answers; the imputation in Goodwin and the uneven dropout in Raison run the same way): low. Rated as worded: larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 weeks (Goodwin, treatment-resistant depression, against a 1-mg dose) and 6 weeks (Raison, mostly non-resistant depression, against niacin) after one 25-mg dose given with psychological support in trials. The claim does not say that the benefit lasts beyond 6 weeks (Goodwin's 12-week sustained response did not differ significantly, and a third of the 25-mg group had started other treatment by then), that 10 mg works (it did not differ from 1 mg), or how psilocybin compares with antidepressants (the separate answer on psilocybin against escitalopram). 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). The response and remission figures of Goodwin are formally not significant because the testing order stopped at the 10-mg comparison, and Raison's sustained response counts only participants assessed at every visit; both are reported as such. Raison's printed relative incidences for related, mild and moderate adverse events do not fit their counts and are not used. Status replicated: two trials with different sponsors, formulations, populations and lead teams point the same way; they share one site (Emory University, Atlanta) and two of its investigators (B. W. Dunlop; T. Mletzko, listed as Mletzko-Crowe in Goodwin) among 22 and 11 sites, which the editors do not count as the same team; the second reader should confirm. Funding and the authors' ties are given as each paper prints them; Goodwin's disclosure forms are not printed and were not read. One published response to Goodwin et al. is now on file: a two-page viewpoint without data of its own (Gukasyan, 2023), by an author of the Raison trial report who declares a co-investigator role on a psilocybin study funded by the Usona Institute (Raison et al., 2023, pp. 843, 851–852). Its two concerns, the missing blinding check and suicidality, are already in the statement and in the rating (risk of bias down two levels), so it changes neither the certainty nor the status. Its framing was checked against the trial's counts (Goodwin et al., 2022, pp. 1637, 1644–1645): events coded as suicidal behaviour (3 participants after week 3) were all in the 25-mg group, as the viewpoint says, but suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, as the trial's abstract states, and worsening of suicidal state by week 3 was most frequent with 10 mg (13 of 75, against 11 of 79 with 25 mg and 7 of 79 with 1 mg); the trial places the suicidal behaviour after week 3, without the one to two months the viewpoint gives, and the viewpoint calls the adverse events relatively high without figures (66 of 79, 56 of 75 and 57 of 79). Published critiques of Raison et al. are not on file; the rating should be revisited when they are (METHODS §2.3).

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

lines.statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Words for the person were tested in one earlier, smaller experiment: of 728 people at talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008 (location not stated), described by the authors as mental health care providers, 516 (mean age 51; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems) completed one of two versions of a story about a man in court-ordered treatment who had positive drug and breath tests; those whose version called him 'a substance abuser' agreed slightly more with a mixed set of statements about blame, punishment, expected violence and religious or other non-medical responses than those whose version said he had 'a substance use disorder' (2.92 against 2.82 on a 1–6 scale; d about 0.2), and did not differ detectably in willingness to have him as an employee, neighbour, co-worker or friend, or in statements about treatment and biological causes (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). That study calls itself randomized, but the two versions were handed out alternately; 29% of those handed a form did not complete it; its printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test (two-sided about .04, above the authors' own threshold of .025); and it could not rule out differences of about the same size in social contact or in the treatment and biological-cause statements. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized; and 516 attendees of talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008, described by the authors as mental health care providers (mean age 51; 64.5% with doctoral-level degrees; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems; Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
lines.exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor); in the second study, a man in court-ordered treatment described as 'a substance abuser' (against as having 'a substance use disorder')
lines.comparator: Readers assigned to the other wording (at random in the pre-registered study; by alternation of the forms in Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
lines.outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task; agreement with a mixed set of blame, punishment, expected-violence and non-medical statements, willingness for social contact, and treatment and biological-cause statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
lines.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), label version vs 'substance use disorder' version: 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58) on a 1–6 scale, t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed as .02 (one-sided by the editors' calculation; two-sided about .041), d printed as 0.20 (about 0.17 to 0.18 recomputed; approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation); 'social threat' (willingness for social contact) and 'victim-treatment' (treatment, genetic and chemical-imbalance causes, severity) subscales, no difference (ps > .59).
lines.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), now read, adds the comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording, in one story and one sample of conference attendees: allocation by alternation and 29% non-completion give it a high risk of bias (card sc_kelly_2010: RoB 2 high), its small difference (d about 0.2, approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation) relies on an unstated one-sided test, and taken alone it would be rated very low; the displayed rating is set by the pre-registered study. Each contrast rests on one study and neither repeats the other, so the status stays single study. Status single study.

lines.q: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?
lines.short: Yes, some do. People judged a person more harshly when their troubles were said to come from drug use, not a health concern.
lines.but: People rated made-up stories. No one checked how people are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, couldn't take part.
When Alex's trouble was put down to drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted much more distance and saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money game, they took slightly more from Alex.
Calling it a brain disease instead of a problem made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested labels on about 500 mental health workers. Calling a man a substance abuser, not someone with a substance use disorder, got slightly more blame and punishment. It's a shaky result.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?

lines.statement: As summarized by a 2010 narrative review (Degenhardt, Bruno, et al., 2010), studies of people who use ecstasy have found that some meet criteria for dependence, but the share ranges from about 4 in 100 to 73 in 100 depending on who was asked, how, and over what period. In two US household surveys, 3.6 in 100 people who had used ecstasy in the past year (Wu et al.) and 3.8 in 100 of those who had started within the previous two years (Stone et al.) met criteria for hallucinogen dependence. In a German community study, 0.4 in 100 of all young adults met past-year criteria for ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence, and 5.8 in 100 of people who had ever used ecstasy had ever met criteria (about 12 of 207 people, by our arithmetic from the table). In samples recruited differently, 19 in 100 of New York nightclub attendees and 22 in 100 of Taiwanese juvenile detainees who used ecstasy met past-year criteria, and 16 to 18 in 100 in convenience samples in Germany, the UK and Australia (195, 1,106 and 1,662 people) were counted as dependent or scored above a screening scale's cut-off. The highest figures, 43, 64 and 73 in 100 over a lifetime, came from three small samples: 52 adolescents and young adults in drug treatment and in the community who had used ecstasy at least 5 times, 185 people the review describes as regularly using ecstasy, and 59 rave attendees who had taken at least 250 tablets in their lifetime. The review says all the instruments were designed for other drugs, only one study used a clinician's assessment, assessment was mostly by self-report and lifetime recall, and most samples were recruited by convenience or snowball methods, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy; it adds that people often reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use and that it is unclear whether they understood the questions as intended, and that pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some dependence may be on another drug. Across studies, the symptoms most often reported included continued use despite problems, spending a lot of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal; in two studies the symptoms fell into a group about compulsive use and a group about escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended). In the one study that followed people (the German community study above), 93 in 100 of those who met criteria at the start no longer did just over three years later and 50 in 100 had stopped using ecstasy altogether; the review does not give the size of that group, which by our arithmetic was about 12 to 14 people. In Australia, fewer than 1 in 100 treatment episodes were for ecstasy. The review also describes animal studies in which MDMA is rewarding but may be less so than other illicit drugs, and notes a lack of case reports of severe withdrawal. It concludes that the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is thin in scope and design.
lines.population: People who use ecstasy in studies summarized by a 2010 narrative review: US and German general-population surveys, New York nightclub attendees, Taiwanese juvenile detainees, and convenience samples in Australia, Germany, the UK and the US (26 to 1,662 people per study)
lines.exposure: Use of ecstasy (pills sold as ecstasy, contents not tested), from a few lifetime occasions to hundreds of tablets
lines.comparator: None in most studies; one study compared ecstasy with other hallucinogens; one followed people over time
lines.outcome: Meeting criteria for dependence on questionnaires or interviews designed for other drugs (DSM-IV hallucinogen or amphetamine criteria, CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale and others), past year, past month or lifetime
lines.magnitude: Share meeting criteria, as printed in Table 1: general population: 3.8% past year (Stone, N 1199, people who started within 2 years), 3.6% past year (Wu, N 652; text says 4%, another 11% with one or two symptoms), 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy (von Sydow, N 207; about 12 people, editors' arithmetic) with 0.4% of all young adults dependent in the past year; sentinel samples: 19% past year (Parsons, N 214), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, N 200); self-selected or convenience samples: 18% past month (Bruno, N 1662, scale cut-off 4 or more), 17% (Winstock, N 1106, scale cut-off 5 or more, timeframe not specified in the table, lifetime in the text), 16% (Tossman, N 195, timeframe not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, N 154, probable dependence), 43% lifetime (Cottler, N 52), 64% lifetime (Topp, N 185), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, N 59, at least 250 lifetime tablets, clinician-rated); Hanson and Luciana (N 26): prevalence cell N = 2 but 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the details column and text. Course (von Sydow, just over 3 years): 93% no longer dependent, 50% no longer using, 43% still using (group size not given; editors' arithmetic: about 12 to 14 people). Treatment: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes. No intervals are given.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive prevalence from observational studies starts low (METHODS 6.3); each of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision takes a level, so the result is very low. That some people meet criteria is better supported than any one percentage. Status replicated in direction only: every study finds some people meeting criteria, while the size varies widely, as the claim states (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim reports findings, makes no statement about risk for any one person and gives no advice.

lines.q: Can people become dependent on ecstasy?
lines.short: Yes, some do. How many depends on who's asked: about 4 in 100 people who'd used it recently in US surveys, but up to 73 in 100 in small groups.
lines.but: Most studies used volunteers and survey forms made for other drugs, so the numbers may not fit everyone.
how: In two US national surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. Among clubgoers, young people in detention and volunteers, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

The symptoms reported most included carrying on despite problems, lots of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.

lines.statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA (study condition; the review does not specify the setting), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were reported in the hormone itself or in blood sodium; the review does not identify that statistical contrast, so it cannot be treated as a demonstrated absence of a sex difference. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 female rows among 52 (88.5 in 100 by editorial calculation, whereas the review prints 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (conditionally 44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation, not a verified unique-patient count), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
lines.population: People with ecstasy intoxication reported to the California Poison Control System in 2000 to 2005 and given a serum sodium result: 188 of 545 included cases (105 women, 83 men; mean age 21 in both); descriptively, 17 UK patients aged 15 to 26 and published case reports tabulated in two narrative reviews; and, as described in the 2020 review, 16 healthy volunteers (8 women, 8 men) in one laboratory study
lines.exposure: Female sex, among people who took ecstasy (MDMA) and became ill; amounts of MDMA and of fluid not recorded
lines.comparator: Men with a recorded sodium; within each sex, people with low sodium against people without
lines.outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L; coma and seizure among those with and without low sodium
lines.magnitude: California poison control, people with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded sodium (Rosenson): low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) in 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%), odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); of the 73 with low sodium, 55 (75.3%) were women, against 296 of 545 (54.3%) women among all cases. Sodium was recorded in 35.3% of women and 33.3% of men. Within each sex, low sodium against not: coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Editors' calculation: 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium among those tested (52.4 minus 21.7). UK series (Hartung): 10 of 17 patients and both deaths female. Earlier series cited by the California paper (not read): 17 of 18 women; 2 of 3 in an Israeli series of 32. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 85% of published symptomatic cases female. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: 46 of 52 rows female (88.5%, editors' calculation; review prints 89%; conditionally omitting two probable duplicates gives 44/50=88.0%, not a verified unique-patient count); controlled crossover, 8 men and 8 women given 125 mg MDMA: copeptin rose in women but not in men, no significant ADH/sodium differences reported, statistical contrast unspecified; postoperative patients with hyponatraemic encephalopathy (Ayus et al., 1992): menstruant women about 25 times as likely to die or have permanent brain injury as men or postmenopausal women. No rate in women or men who take MDMA can be derived.
lines.reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference among reported cases; the UK series and the two reviews are consistent but do not test it, and both reviews' tables overlap the California series. The 2020 review (Faria et al.; card sc_faria_2020) infers a female predisposition from its case counts, but its table has errors and no denominators, and the only controlled comparison it describes (Simmler et al., 2011, not read) reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the statistical contrast; that study and the postoperative data (Ayus et al., 1992, not read) are second-hand. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.

lines.q: Is low blood salt after MDMA more common in women?
lines.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
lines.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.
